title: Sleep, Chronotype and Physiological Acclimatisation During a 21-Day Altitude Training Camp in World-Class Swimmers.
abstract: Altitude training is widely used in elite swimming, although its effects on sleep and acclimatisation remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to describe changes in sleep difficulty, physiological acclimatisation, athlete-reported outcomes, and haematological markers during a 21-day altitude training camp (2320 m), and to explore the association between chronotype and sleep difficulty. Seven world-class swimmers (4 men, 3 women) were monitored before, during, and after altitude exposure. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire, while daily monitoring included resting oxygen saturation, resting heart rate, acute mountain sickness symptoms, fatigue, recovery, hydration status, and training load. Chronotype was determined using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire. Sleep difficulty was descriptively higher during the first week at altitude (6.14 ± 1.07 vs. 4.14 ± 1.21 at baseline) and returned towards baseline by week 3 (4.29 ± 1.50), although pairwise comparisons did not remain significant after multiplicity correction. Strong inverse associations between chronotype and sleep difficulty were observed at baseline (rho = -0.87, p = 0.014) and week 1 (rho = -0.85, p = 0.019), but neither met the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold (α = 0.010). SpO2 increased across the camp, with week 3 significantly higher than weeks 1 and 2 after Bonferroni correction, whereas RHR was significantly lower in week 3 than in week 1, but not week 2, after correction. Athlete-reported outcomes remained stable, acute mountain sickness symptoms were minimal, and haematological and iron-status markers showed no significant pre-to-post changes. Sleep difficulty showed a transient descriptive increase during the initial phase of the altitude camp, while SpO2 and RHR changes were consistent with physiological acclimatisation. Chronotype-related differences in sleep difficulty appeared to be present before altitude exposure rather than emerging specifically during the camp. Given the small sample size, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

title: Multidimensional Pre-Competition Stress Profiles in Wheelchair Basketball: Associations with Cortisol and Psychological Indicators.
abstract: This study examined pre-competition cortisol levels and psychological anticipation in wheelchair basketball athletes using a person-centred approach. Thirty-four male athletes (mean age: 35 ± 7.75 years) competing in a regional league provided saliva samples 35-50 min before competition and completed psychological assessments with the Revised Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2R) and the Perceived Stress Scale. K-Means cluster analysis (k = 3), validated by Ward's hierarchical clustering (ARI = 0.947; NMI = 0.892) and Bootstrap Jaccard stability (0.544-0.603), identified three exploratory stress profiles: Low Reactor (n = 5; low cortisol, anxiety, and stress), High Reactor (n = 20; moderate cortisol, high cognitive/physical anxiety), and Physiological Stress Reactor (n = 9; high cortisol, high stress, moderate anxiety). Significant group differences were observed for log(Cortisol) (H(2) = 17.095, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.518), Cognitive Anxiety (H(2) = 13.900, p < 0.01, ε2 = 0.421), Somatic Anxiety (H(2) = 18.840, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.571), and Perceived Stress (H(2) = 21.831, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.662), while self-confidence did not differ. Exploratory logistic regression indicated that functional classification, years of sport participation, match location, and match result did not significantly predict the Physiological Stress Reactor membership. These findings suggest that pre-competition stress-related characteristics may manifest in different combinations of physiological and psychological indicators. The identified profiles should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger and independent samples.

title: Breaking limits: rapid sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) in 3 days 23 hours following normobaric-hypoxic pre-acclimatization and staged supplemental oxygen in a non-elite athlete.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Traditional ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) typically requires 40-50 days of on-mountain acclimatization. Normobaric hypoxia (NH) pre-acclimatization is a practical home-based alternative; however, no peer-reviewed case report has described a sea-to-summit Everest ascent completed in under four days by a non-elite individual without prior on-mountain acclimatization rotations.
METHODS: A 40-year-old male recreational mountaineer (baseline VO2max 40.8 ml·kg-1·min-1; BMI 30.1 kg·m-2) completed an 18-week structured NH pre-acclimatization program comprising 48 nights of hypoxic sleep (~377 h at simulated altitudes of 1,850-5,486 m; FiO2 16.7-10.5%) and 16 hypoxic exercise sessions (34 h at 3,085-6,000 m; FiO2 14.3-9.8%). Hypoxic dose was calculated as Σ[(95/SpO2 - 1) × h × 100]. During the climb, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at each camp, and acute mountain sickness (AMS) was assessed using the 2018 Lake Louise Score (LLS). Supplemental oxygen (O2) was initiated at 0.5 L·min-1 at the start of the ascent from Everest Base Camp (EBC, 5,360 m) and titrated to SpO2 and symptoms up to 3.0 L·min-1 during the summit push.
RESULTS: The program yielded a combined hypoxic exposure of 411 h and a cumulative hypoxic dose of 4,779%·h (sleep 4,353%·h; exercise 426%·h). VO2max increased from 40.8 to 51.0 ml·kg-1·min-1, and body mass decreased from 118.1 to 101.5 kg. The subject departed New York at 00:30 local time (EDT; 10:15 Nepal Standard Time, NST) on 15 May 2025 and reached the summit at 09:22 NST on 19 May 2025, a total sea-to-summit time of 3 days, 23 hours and 7 minutes; the ascent from EBC to the summit took 60 hours and 22 minutes. SpO2 was 75% at Camp 3 (7,100 m; HR 95 bpm) and 70% on arrival at Camp 4 (7,950 m; HR 105 bpm) and at the summit (HR 105 bpm). On descent, SpO2 recovered to 80% at Camp 4 and 85% at Camp 2 (6,750 m; HR 110 bpm), and was 85% on room air on return to EBC (HR 62 bpm). No AMS was diagnosed during the ascent (LLS 0-1 at all ascending checkpoints); mild AMS criteria were met on descent (LLS = 3), resolving by return to EBC. No high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary edema occurred.
DISCUSSION: To our knowledge, this case documents the fastest recorded sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest by a non-professional athlete. The combination of a structured 18-week NH pre-acclimatization program, objective physiological monitoring, and staged supplemental oxygen, together with the absence of severe altitude-related complications, suggests that rapid ascent without traditional on-mountain acclimatization may be feasible in a well-prepared, closely supervised non-elite individual. Controlled prospective studies are required to quantify the relative contributions of hematological, ventilatory, and mitochondrial adaptations induced by high-dose NH exposure.

title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated.
METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours.
RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones.
CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Application of FTIR to detect changes in blood plasma during a pre-competition period in a professional heavyweight boxer.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES AND DESIGN: This exploratory single-case study examined whether repeated attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy of blood plasma is technically feasible during a short pre-competition period and whether spectral regions co-vary with conventionally assayed biochemical markers.
METHODS: One professional heavyweight boxer was monitored over a 13-day pre-competition period characterized by reduced training load (tapering). Morning fasting blood was collected on five occasions (10, 13, 17, 20, and 23 May 2024) into lithium-heparin tubes and centrifuged to obtain plasma. Creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP), glucose, cortisol, testosterone, total and reduced glutathione, malondialdehyde, and zinc were quantified by conventional laboratory assays; ATR-FTIR spectra were acquired separately from the same plasma aliquots and were not used to quantify any of these analytes. Each plasma sample was measured eight times, yielding 40 spectra from five biological observations; the technical replicates are presented to illustrate within-sample visual consistency. Associations between the intensities of 22 spectral peaks and 12 biochemical variables were explored using Pearson correlation.
RESULTS: Plasma biochemical parameters showed changes during the pre-competition tapering period, including decreases in CK and CRP and increases in glutathione and testosterone, whereas cortisol remained relatively stable. FTIR spectra exhibited consistent vibrational profiles with changes in selected band intensities over time. Linear regression identified strong associations between glutathione levels and FTIR bands at 671, 699, and 721 cm-1 (R 2 = 0.80-0.92), as well as between cortisol and the 3,009 cm-1 band (R 2 = 0.77). Because of the limited number of observations (n = 5), these findings are preliminary and require validation in larger cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated plasma measurements using ATR-FTIR demonstrated technical feasibility and visual consistency during a short pre-competition period in the studied athlete, while identifying potential spectral regions worthy of further investigation. The obtained results should be treated as preliminary. However, they do not provide evidence that ATR-FTIR enables the quantitative determination of glutathione or cortisol, or that it can be used to assess an athlete's competitive readiness. Confirmation of such capabilities requires studies involving adequately large and diverse groups of participants.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: Long-Term Fitness Profile and Performance-Related Indicators in Semi-Professional Female Handball Players.
abstract: Long-term, single-club datasets linking fitness and match performance are rare in women's handball. This retrospective study profiled fitness and game-quality indicators across 14 seasons (2010-2022, 2026; N = 45; 8-17 players/season). Anthropometric and specific-fitness values (height 173.90 ± 5.53 cm, body mass 68.28 ± 8.08 kg, jump-throw velocity 79.94 ± 6.83 km/h, countermovement jump 43.46 ± 4.84 cm, VO2max 48.01 ± 3.61 mL/kg/min) were sub-elite. Shot efficiency (55.74 ± 6.00%) approached elite values (58.90 ± 7.60%). Backs were older, more experienced, and higher-scoring than Wings and Pivots. Universal players matched Backs' output despite being younger and less experienced. Experience correlated with goals per match (r = 0.51, p = 0.001), positive actions (r = 0.44, p = 0.005), and action balance (r = 0.47, p = 0.003). Throwing velocity and sprint/agility speed showed similar associations. Endurance, strength, and coordination/dribble deficit showed none. Fitness indicators improved across 2010-2022, but a single season after near-complete roster turnover departed markedly from this trend. Trends should not be extrapolated to a changed roster without retesting. A small set of trainable, sport-specific qualities, not general fitness, best predicts match performance. Findings provide normative benchmarks and training priorities for coaches.

title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs).
METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests.
RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

title: Progression of peak athletic performance age in the past four decades.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older athletes are redefining the prime by extending their athletic longevity. A trend that women's peak performance age tends to increase, while men's remains largely unchanged, has been reported some time ago. The present study builds on this early work by examining more recent data to determine whether such gender differences persisted across contemporary periods and in different sporting events.
METHODS: Ages of Olympic medalists from 1984 to 2024 were analyzed as indicators of peak performance age (N.=2016).
RESULTS: In men, peak performance ages ranged 26±2 to 28±2 years in endurance, 26±2 to 27±2 years in power, 23±1 to 24±2 years in sprint, and 26±2 to 27±2 years in skill. In women, the ranges were from 27±2 to 29±2 years for endurance, 26±2 to 28±2 years for power, 23±2 to 24±2 years for sprint, and 23±3 to 26±3 years for skill. There were no gender differences in peak performance age among endurance, power, and sprint events in any era. However, in skill sports, male athletes demonstrated a higher peak performance age in 1984-1996 (P<0.05), a difference that has since disappeared. The age variabilities show an upward trend over time in both men and women.
CONCLUSIONS: We concluded that in recent years, both male and female athletes have achieved peak performance at comparable ages across all sport types.
journal: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness

title: Young Investigator Award: Where Do We Start? A Conceptual Model for Implementing Menstrual Cycle Tracking in Sport.
abstract: Menstrual cycle tracking is a much-discussed component of the ' female athlete' research theme; however, more translational work is needed to meet practitioners' desire for further guidance on the implementation of tracking in applied settings. The purpose of this paper is to present a preliminary conceptual model to inform practitioners' decision-making around menstrual cycle tracking and assist researchers in identifying and framing future research directions. The proposed model-Conducting and Navigating menstrual cycle Education, Communication and Tracking (ConNECT)-proposes that communication and education strategies may be utilised to affect social, organisational and individual level change, ultimately supporting the implementation of menstrual cycle tracking by increasing its uptake and impact. This model was developed based on the findings from a series of studies conducted by the authors, which considered the existing literature on tracking and the perspectives of athletes and practitioners. Therefore, the ConNECT model offers an ecologically sound starting point for sport scientists, coaches and other members of an athlete's support team to base their practice on.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Gamified Versus Traditional Balance Training: Effects on Balance and Motivation in Collegiate Student-Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gamified balance platforms offer engaging alternatives to traditional balance tools; however, their comparative effectiveness in improving dynamic balance and motivation in athletic populations remains unclear.Hypothesis/Purpose: To compare the effects of gamified (Wii Fit) versus traditional (wobble board) balance training on dynamic balance and intrinsic motivation in collegiate athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Quasi-experimental controlled trial.
METHODS: Thirty healthy collegiate athletes (5 males, 25 females; 19.8 ± 0.9 years) were pseudo-randomized to gamified training (n = 9), traditional training (n = 11), or a control group (n = 10). Participants in the training groups completed twelve 15-minute supervised sessions (three times per week for four weeks). Dynamic balance was assessed pre- and post-intervention using the modified Star Excursion Balance Test (mSEBT) and the Dynamic Postural Stability Index (DPSI). Motivation was evaluated post-training using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI). Group x time differences were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests, and IMI scores were compared between training groups using one-way ANOVAs.
RESULTS: Both training groups showed significant improvements in anterior reach (gamified: +6.5 ± 10.2 cm; traditional: +6.5 ± 10.3 cm) and mSEBT composite scores (gamified: +21.6 ± 11.9 cm, d = 1.84; traditional: +18.5 ± 14.6 cm, d = 1.54) compared with control (-2.3 ± 10.5 cm; p < 0.01). DPSI scores did not change significantly (p > 0.28). IMI interest/enjoyment scores were higher in the gamified group (5.0 ± 1.2) than the traditional group (3.2 ± 1.3; p < 0.01, d = 1.50).
CONCLUSION: Gamified balance training produced similar biomechanical improvements to traditional balance training while eliciting greater enjoyment. It may serve as an engaging option for balance rehabilitation and injury-prevention programs in athletes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 2.

title: Post-COVID-19 Penalty Trends Following an Injury-Prevention Rule Change in Rhode Island High School Boys' Hockey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Penalty infraction minute (PIM)-based rule modifications have been implemented in youth and high school ice hockey to reduce injury risk. A prior Rhode Island Interscholastic League (RIIL) study demonstrated a reduction in game-related injuries following implementation of a statewide 2015-2016 50/70 PIM rule. The durability of these behavioral trends post-COVID-19 has not been evaluated.
PURPOSE: This descriptive epidemiologic study evaluates post-pandemic trends in penalty infraction minutes and disqualifying penalties in RIIL boys' varsity ice hockey.
METHODS: Publicly available RIIL varsity boys' ice hockey data were reviewed for four consecutive seasons (2021-2022 through 2024-2025). Extracted variables included total rostered players, counts of players exceeding PIM thresholds (≥25, ≥50, ≥70), mean team PIM per game, goals scored, number of participating teams, and total disqualifying penalties per season. Data were summarized descriptively by season.
RESULTS: Across four seasons, rostered players ranged from 479 to 540, with 21 to 25 teams competing annually. Mean team PIM per game remained stable, ranging from 8.13 to 8.83. No players accumulated ≥50 or ≥70 PIM in any season. Players accumulating ≥25 PIM ranged from 17 to 24 per season. Disqualifying penalties occurred each season (range, 5-11 per year) without a consistent directional trend. Goals scored remained proportional to participating teams.
CONCLUSIONS: In post-pandemic seasons, PIM distributions and disqualifying penalties remained stable, with no recurrence of high-PIM accumulations requiring suspension. These findings suggest sustained behavioral patterns following rule modifications, but cannot be interpreted as evidence of injury reduction without injury surveillance data. Continued monitoring incorporating injury outcomes is warranted.

title: Return-to-Play Outcomes After Primary Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Vary Substantially Depending on Return Criteria: A Systematic Review Stratified by Competition Level.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine how return definitions influence return to play (RTP), return to the same level of play (RTSP), advancement rates, and return timelines after primary ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (UCLR) in baseball pitchers across levels of competition.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from January 2000 to January 2025. Studies evaluating baseball pitchers undergoing primary UCLR and reporting RTP, RTSP, advancement, or return timing outcomes with participation-based (RTP based on a single event) or durability-based (RTP after sustained participation over a predefined threshold) criteria were included. Primary outcomes were RTP, RTSP, and advancement rate (progression to a higher level after UCLR); secondary outcome was return time stratified by return criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with the Methodological Index for Non-randomized Studies and Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met inclusion. Across these studies, 19 included Major League Baseball players (2194 players), 5 included Minor League Baseball (MiLB) players (2318 players), 4 included collegiate athletes (553 athletes), and 6 included high school athletes (258 athletes). RTP/RTSP rates were 86% to 92%/70% to 87% in high school, 84%/67% to 92% in college, 76.3% to 79%/69.1% to 100% in MiLB, and 80% to 97.2%/28.1% to 87% in Major League Baseball. Advancement was 55.7% to 63.2% in high school, 4.1% to 44.4% in college, and 22.3% to 45% in MiLB. Surgery-to-return time using the common RTSP definition ranged from 13.7 to 20.5 months (Major League Baseball), 14.6 to 16.4 (MiLB), and 11 to 17 (college and high school). Durability-based definitions were not consistently associated with longer return intervals.
CONCLUSIONS: Without standardized return criteria, reported RTP, RTSP, advancement rates, and return timelines after primary UCLR in baseball pitchers varied substantially across studies and competition levels. Durability-based criteria were not consistently associated with longer return timelines, indicating that return outcomes should be interpreted according to the competition level and return definition used. Standardized, tier-specific return criteria may improve clinical interpretation after primary UCLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: The Effect of a Bioactive Fabric Sleeve on Flexor-Pronator Recovery in Collegiate Baseball Pitchers: A Pilot Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fatigue of the flexor-pronator mass could lead to increased stresses on the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) and potential injury. Soreness is a clinical indicator of fatigue. If flexor-pronator soreness recovery could be improved, there is potential protection of the UCL in baseball throwers. Hypothesis/Purpose The purpose of this study was to investigate the efficacy of a bioactive fabric sleeve in enhancing subjective recovery in high-level pitchers who experience soft tissue soreness around the elbow. The investigators hypothesized that the use of the bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve would lead to a significant reduction in subjective elbow soreness the day following in-game pitching competition.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort pilot study.
METHODS: Health Division I collegiate baseball pitchers were recruited to participate. The intervention consisted of two sleeve types: a control standard elbow compression sleeve and the experimental bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve, worn the night after their pitching performance to bed and removed the following morning. The main outcome measure was subjective reported soreness in the soft tissues of the medial elbow reported the night of and the day after the pitching appearance in a collegiate baseball game. The length of the study encompassed the duration of the spring baseball season, allowing for multiple evaluations throughout the pitchers' regular game schedules. A multivariable mixed-effects linear regression model was used to analyze changes in subjective pain and soreness between the bioactive, non-compressive, fabric sleeve and control sleeves, adjusting for time of season and accounting for multiple data points per pitcher.
RESULTS: The bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve resulted in a statistically significant reduction in subjective reporting of pain the morning after pitching compared with reported pain the night of pitching (p=0.044) versus the change associated with a control sleeve.
CONCLUSION: This study showed the bioactive fabric was safe and demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in subjective reporting of medial elbow pain. Successful implementation of the study design was accomplished with high-level baseball pitchers. Future studies should involve a greater number of athletes with more granular assessment considering actual pitching workload.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II.

title: Effects of Blood Flow Restriction Training on Pain Perception in Athletes with Sacroiliac Joint Dysfunction: A Case Series.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) dysfunction is a common cause of non-specific low back pain (LBP), affecting up to 30% of the patient population. While various conservative and invasive treatments are available, many pose risks or are poorly tolerated. Blood Flow Restriction (BFR) training promotes strength gains with low-load resistance, offering a potential alternative to promote SIJ stabilization and strengthen surrounding musculature in patients who cannot tolerate traditional high-load exercises due to pain.
PURPOSE: To describe the preliminary clinical outcomes specifically regarding pain, function, and disability in a small series of subjects with SIJ dysfunction following a single session of BFR training.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series.
METHODS: Four subjects with clinically confirmed SIJ dysfunction using the Cluster of Laslett underwent a single BFR training session using the Delfi Personal Tourniquet System, performing low-load bodyweight squats under 80% arterial occlusion for 4 sets of 30, 15, 15, 15, as outlined by Owens Recovery Sciences. Outcomes were measured using the Numerical Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS), and Disablement in the Physically Active Scale Short Form-8 (DPA SF-8), recorded before treatment, immediately after, and at one-week follow-up.
RESULTS: All subjects experienced complete pain relief (NPRS = 0) immediately post-treatment and at follow-up. PSFS scores increased by an average of 7.63 points. DPA SF-8 scores improved from a mean of 25.75 to 0, reflecting significant gains in function and quality of life.
CONCLUSION: A single BFR session produced immediate and short-term improvements in pain, function, and disability in four subjects with SIJ dysfunction.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
abstract: Wei, X, Zhu, H, Zheng, X, Gao, Y, Huang, J, Chen, X, Vigh-Larsen, JF, Mohr, M, and Krustrup, P. Greater reductions in deceleration compared with sprint ability following repeated high-intensity exercise in male and female soccer players, but no effect on countermovement jump (CMJ) or ball-kicking performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the acute effect of repeated sprint and deceleration on the fatigue of each component (sprint vs. deceleration) and on CMJ and soccer kicking performance, and to investigate the association between deceleration ability and fatigue. Thirty-three high-level male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) college soccer players completed 10 × 15-m sprints with subsequent 5-m enforced deceleration, interspersed with 20-s recovery intervals. Sprint and deceleration performance were measured continuously during the protocol, while CMJ and kicking performance were assessed before and immediately after. Furthermore, the players' deceleration ability was measured using deceleration deficit and deceleration index. Peak deceleration had significantly higher fatigue index (FI) and decrement score (Sdec) compared with speed (p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 3.18-3.32), while no significant decline was found in CMJ or kicking performance after the repeated sprint and deceleration protocol (p > 0.05, Cohen's d = -0.06∼0.23). A significant repeated sprint and deceleration × sex interaction effect was observed in peak ball speed (p < 0.05, ηp2 = 0.149), with women showing a decrease in peak ball speed compared with their male counterparts. The deceleration index correlated with FI and Sdec of speed (r = -0.444∼-0.516, p < 0.05), and the rate of CMJ decline correlated with FI and Sdec deceleration (r = 0.530-0.549, p < 0.05). Finally, the rate of decline in kicking speed was positively correlated with the Sdec deceleration rate (r = 0.423, p < 0.05). Deceleration capacity is more prone to acute fatigue than sprint ability. In addition, repeated sprint and deceleration had a limited effect on athletic performance, but men and women showed different adjusted trends in kicking speed. Finally, players having better deceleration capacity show a smaller performance drop.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
abstract: Villaseca-Vicuña, R, Freitas, TT, Spyrou, K, Marín-Cascales, E, Comyns, T, Loturco, I, and Zabaloy, S. Countermovement jump performance across 10 competitive microcycles in under-18 soccer players: An analysis of delayed and long-term responses to training and official competition. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aims of this study were to (a) determine within-microcycle changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) measures (i.e., jump height, reactive strength index modified [RSImod], and eccentric peak velocity [EPV]) collected 2 days after (MD+2) and 1 day before (MD-1) the match-day across 10 weeks during the competitive period in under-18 soccer players and (b) analyze week-to-week variations in the selected CMJ-metrics collected on MD+2 across the entire mesocycle. Twelve (n = 12) under-18 academy soccer players (age: 17.5 ± 0.5 years; body mass: 71.9 ± 7.7 kg) volunteered to participate in this study. Over 10 competitive weeks, CMJ assessments were recorded on force plates at 2 key microcycle time points: MD+2 (active recovery phase at the start of the microcycle) and MD-1 (end of the microcycle). Results showed significant within-week changes in CMJ height and EPV in most of the training microcycles (p: <0.001 to 0.049) while RSImod showed significant changes in only 4 of the 10 microcycles (p: 0.001 to 0.049). Similarly, the between-week comparisons showed significant variations only in EPV and RSI (p: 0.005 to 0.049). These findings suggest that jump height might be better suited to assess within-week changes, while RSImod appears to hold greater discriminative value for detecting between-week fluctuations. Eccentric peak velocity, in turn, may provide useful information for both within-week and between-week changes in young soccer players.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Conservative and Post-Operative Rehabilitation Protocols for Hip Dysplasia in Adolescents to Adulthood: A Literature Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a spectrum of structural abnormalities associated with insufficient acetabular coverage, predisposing adults to labral pathology, chondral wear, and early-onset osteoarthritis. Despite a range of conservative and post-operative management options, key aspects of physiotherapy rehabilitation remain poorly defined, including intervention timing, progressive loading criteria and exercise selection in those with DDH. The purpose of this review is to examine conservative and post-operative rehabilitation protocols and associated functional outcomes in adolescents and adults aged 13-50 years with DDH.
METHODS: A structured electronic search of MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science Core Collection was used to identify English-language, peer-reviewed literature addressing physiotherapy rehabilitation for DDH. Twelve sources met inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, Delphi consensus studies, a retrospective case series, and observational designs. Data were extracted regarding intervention type, progression criteria, patient-reported outcome measures, and return to sport measures.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Twelve sources were included, comprising adolescent and adult cohorts aged 13-50 years, with one source exclusively including an adolescent population aged 5-17 years.1 Conservative rehabilitation commonly emphasised hip abductor, extensor and hip external rotator strengthening combined with lumbopelvic stability and movement pattern retraining. Post-operative protocols applied phased, criterion-based progressions guided by pain-free range of motion, ≥80% hip abductor strength symmetry, and functional stability testing. The overall evidence base was limited by methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, reliance on expert consensus, with no high-quality comparative trials identified.
CONCLUSION: Current evidence tentatively supports physiotherapy as a central component of both conservative and post-operative rehabilitation for adolescents and adults with DDH, with multimodal, criterion-based approaches incorporating progressive strengthening and neuromuscular retraining most consistently described across included sources. Standardized rehabilitation frameworks and validated progression criteria are needed to optimize functional outcomes in this population.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 5.
journal: International journal of sports physical therapy

title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern.
PURPOSE: To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective case series.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications.
RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable.
LEVEL OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE: 4.
