title: Different osteoarthritis progression rates within early-stage knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective cohort study using machine learning cluster analysis from the osteoarthritis initiative database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disease with varying progression rates among patients within the same severity grade. This study aimed to identify clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes among knees with baseline Kellgren and Lawrence (KL) grade 2 osteoarthritis and to compare their 4-year radiographic progression patterns using baseline radiographic features, lifetime exercise patterns, and demographic characteristics.
METHODS: Data of patients with baseline KL grade 2 from the Osteoarthritis Initiative database were retrieved. Unsupervised clustering was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) for dimensionality reduction, followed by hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) to identify distinct subgroups. The proportion of knees progressing to KL grade ≥ 3 within 4 years was compared between subgroups, followed by a survival analysis until knee replacement or progression to KL grade 4.
RESULTS: A total of 1997 knees with a mean follow-up of 103.3 months (maximum, 108 months) were included. A total of seven subgroups were identified and classified into accelerated osteoarthritis progression (AOP) group and slow osteoarthritis progression (SOP) group according to whether their 4-year KL grade progression proportions were above or below the training-set average. In a supportive long-term survival analysis, the AOP group also showed significantly earlier progression to knee replacement or KL grade 4 than the SOP group (training set, P < 0.001; test set, P = 0.049), although the absolute difference in mean survival time was modest (8.3 versus 8.5 years in the training set; 8.4 versus 8.6 years in the test set). The AOP group was characterized mainly by lateral joint space narrowing (JSN) and medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, whereas the SOP group was characterized by medial JSN without subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant patterns without JSN, or chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns; these differences were statistically significant across clusters.
CONCLUSIONS: Within baseline KL grade 2 knees, clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes, including lateral JSN, medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant changes without JSN, and chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns, were associated with different 4-year KL grade progression rates. These findings support viewing KL grade 2 knee OA as a heterogeneous radiographic stage that may be further stratified into phenotype-based subgroups with different short-term radiographic prognoses.

title: Osteoarthritis-Microenvironment-Triggered Phase Alteration of Injectable Conductive Hydrogel for Attenuating Cartilage Degradation.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is associated with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which contributes substantially to chondrocyte dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cartilage degradation. Although stimuli-responsive hydrogels have emerged as promising platforms for OA therapy, conventional hydrogel-based systems exhibit limited sensitivity and require external detection equipment, highlighting the need for a simple, sensitive, and directly observable monitoring system. To address these challenges, we developed a ROS-triggered, in situ-forming gel-sol transition of a polydopamine (PDA)-loaded, diselenide-crosslinked polymer dot (PD) injectable hydrogel (HGC-PDA@PD or OA gel) as a monitorable theranostic for OA therapy at physiological temperature (37°C). The monitorable OA microenvironment-responsive hydrogel relied on interactions between the high ROS levels in OA cartilage and the OA gel, which triggered diselenide bond cleavage and the release of PDA from PD, causing a unique gel-sol transition of the OA gel. Owing to PDA release after diselenide breakage, the fluorescence and electroconductivity of the OA gel changed, which could serve as additional signals during OA detection. In vitro studies demonstrated the sensitive gel-sol transition of OA gel towards OA-induced immature articular chondrocytes (IL-1β/siSOD1/siCatalase-transfected iMACs). Furthermore, the OA gel showed a distinct gel-sol transition in cartilage of an in vivo OA mouse model compared with that in control mice. The lower transcription levels of cartilage matrix-degrading enzymes (ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, MMP-3, and MMP-13) observed after OA gel injection confirmed that the OA gel could scavenge ROS and attenuate cartilage damage, revealing its potential application for dual-function OA diagnosis and rehabilitation.

title: High Survival and Continued Sports Participation After Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Athletes With and Without Lateral Rim Dysplasia With Minimum 4.5-Year Follow-Up.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To quantify the outcomes, including sporting capability, of hip arthroscopy (HA) in athletes for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) in the presence of concomitant lateral rim dysplasia (LR-Dysplasia) compared with a matched athletic control group.
METHODS: Athletes undergoing unilateral primary HA for FAI with or without LR-Dysplasia between January 2009 and May 2020 were considered. All athletes with a lateral center-edge angle of <25° on anteroposterior view were matched to those with normal overcoverage (lateral center-edge angle >30°). Patients were contacted a minimum of 4.5 years after the procedure. Outcomes included survival (avoidance of total hip replacement), revision HA, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) consisting of the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity score, 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Substantial clinical benefit thresholds were determined for each PROM, and the proportion of cases achieving substantial clinical benefit was compared between groups. Finally, the ability to continue to play sports and satisfaction were determined.
RESULTS: Forty-eight patients with LR-Dysplasia were matched to 97 controls with a mean follow-up of 72 ± 19 months (54-120 months). At follow-up, survival was 100% in the LR-Dysplasia group versus 99% in controls. The revision HA rates were 6% in LR-Dysplasia patients and 9% in controls. Both groups showed significant improvements in PROMs. In the LR-Dysplasia group, mHHS improved from 82 to 100 (P < .001), UCLA from 8 to 9 (P = .114), SF-36 from 74 to 87 (P = .002), and WOMAC from 15 to 2 (P < .001). In the control group, mHHS improved from 82 to 96 (P < .001), UCLA from 7 to 10 (P = .003), SF-36 from 72 to 89 (P < .001), and WOMAC from 17 to 4 (P = .005). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences in pre- or postoperative mHHS (P = .498; P = .183), UCLA (P = .684; P = .388), SF-36 (P = .487; P = .602), or WOMAC (P = .814; P = .390). Substantial clinical benefit was achieved by most patients for each PROM and similar between groups (P > .05 for all). No significant differences were observed between groups in PROMs or overall satisfaction with surgery (P > .05 for all). Sports participation at 5 years was 84% in the LR-Dysplasia group and 90% in controls (P = .103).
CONCLUSIONS: In the absence of arthritic changes, athletes treated with arthroscopy for FAI where LR-Dysplasia is present showed high survival rates and improved pain and function. Furthermore, most athletes can maintain their preoperative levels of sport. Importantly, the outcomes observed in this specific patient cohort are comparable to those seen in athletes with normal acetabular coverage, indicating that the presence of LR-Dysplasia does not compromise the effectiveness of arthroscopic intervention for FAI in athletes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.
journal: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Analgesic efficacy of regional and local analgesic techniques for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in adults undergoing general anesthesia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute pain after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) can impair early mobility and rehabilitation. This network meta-analysis (NMA) compared regional and local analgesic techniques in adults undergoing ACLR under general anesthesia.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 18, 2026, for randomized controlled trials. Risk of bias was assessed utilizing the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB2), and a Bayesian random-effects NMA was performed.
RESULTS: Thirty-one studies involving 2,470 patients were included. Only six were at low risk of bias. For oral morphine milligram equivalents (OMME) at 24 h postoperatively, femoral nerve block (FNB) [mean difference (MD) = - 30.31, 95% credible interval (CrI) - 58.02, - 6.79] and FNB with sciatic nerve block (SNB) [MD = - 40.42, 95% CrI - 80.42, - 5.79] were associated with lower estimated opioid consumption than control. FNB with SNB ranked highest for lower 24-h OMME [surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) = 87.44%]. FNB with graft donor-site infiltration was associated with lower estimated pain scores in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) than local infiltration analgesia (MD = - 2.46, 95% CrI: -4.67, - 0.21). At 24 h, adductor canal block (ACB) with graft donor-site infiltration had lower estimated pain scores than ACB (MD = - 1.50, 95% CrI: -2.43, - 0.61). At 48 h, the 95% CrIs for all pain comparisons included 0. ACB with infiltration between the popliteal artery and capsule of the posterior knee (iPACK) had a longer estimated time to first analgesic request (TFAR) than ACB (MD = 7.50, 95% CrI: 1.92, 13.01). Regarding postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), the 95% CrIs for all comparisons included 1. In sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk studies, the CrIs for key comparisons regarding OMME and TFAR widened and included 0. Some treatment nodes were missing from certain outcome networks, and the rankings for PONV changed.
CONCLUSION: Potential analgesic benefits varied across outcomes, but key estimates became less precise after high-risk studies were excluded. Functional outcomes were not systematically synthesized, and adverse event assessment was limited to PONV. These findings do not establish the overall clinical superiority of any single strategy.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: Meniscal Repair Achieves Comparable Mid-Term Functional Performance to Partial Meniscectomy Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Highly Active Patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Concomitant meniscal injuries accompany 40%-60% of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures. Surgeons often face a clinical choice between meniscal repair, which prioritizes long-term joint preservation, and partial meniscectomy, which is traditionally perceived to facilitate earlier functional recovery. Despite the biological advantages of repair, persistent concerns remain that its restrictive postoperative protocols might impede mid-term functional performance compared to meniscectomy. This study aims to compare quadriceps/hamstring strength, dynamic balance, functional hop performance, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) at 2-5 years post-ACLR between patients undergoing concomitant meniscal repair versus partial meniscectomy.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated highly active patients who underwent ACLR between 2019 and 2023. Of 68 patients who underwent ACLR with a concomitant meniscal injury and a pre-injury Tegner score ≥ 6,16 were excluded: 5 due to revision ACLR or secondary meniscal procedures during the follow-up period, 8 due to concurrent multi-ligament injuries or full-thickness articular cartilage defects requiring surgery, and 3 due to knee joint deformities (varus or valgus malalignment > 5°)The remaining 52 patients were stratified into meniscal repair (n = 20) or partial meniscectomy (n = 32) groups. Outcomes included isokinetic strength (60°/s, 180°/s; Limb Symmetry Index, LSI), Y-balance test, single-leg hop (SLH), and PROMs (IKDC, Lysholm, and ACL-RSI).
RESULTS: At mid-term follow-up (mean 4.1 ± 1.2 years for repair, 4.2 ± 1.2 years for meniscectomy; p = 0.59), no significant differences existed in strength (quadriceps/hamstring LSI 60°/s and 180°/s), dynamic balance (Y-balance), hop tests (SLH, SLCH, and SLTH), or PROMs (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: At mid-term follow-up (2-5 years), concomitant meniscal repair yielded objective functional performance and patient-reported outcomes equivalent to partial meniscectomy in highly active patients undergoing ACLR, despite more restrictive early rehabilitation. These findings indicate that the initial postoperative restrictions associated with repair do not result in persistent functional deficits. Although meniscal preservation confers established long-term chondroprotective advantages, the present analysis addresses functional parity only; the surgical strategy should weigh both mid-term function and long-term joint health on an individual basis.

title: Has Modern Tennis Changed the Mechanical Environment of the Elbow? A Narrative Review and the Cumulative Elbow Load Model.
abstract: Upper-extremity injuries are common in tennis and are predominantly associated with repetitive mechanical loading. Modern professional tennis has evolved substantially, with greater topspin production, higher racquet-head speeds, prolonged baseline exchanges, increased physical demands, and dense competitive schedules. These changes may influence the cumulative mechanical environment experienced by the upper extremity. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence regarding elbow injury risk in tennis, with particular attention to workload, stroke biomechanics, fatigue, kinetic-chain function, recovery capacity, and tennis ball characteristics. The available literature supports a multifactorial perspective in which stroke volume, stroke intensity, topspin demand, fatigue accumulation, and equipment-related factors may interact to influence cumulative mechanical exposure, while recovery capacity and kinetic-chain efficiency may modify the athlete's ability to tolerate and adapt to repeated loading. Based on these concepts, the authors propose the Cumulative Elbow Load Model (CELM), a conceptual framework in which elbow symptoms and injury may occur when cumulative mechanical exposure persistently exceeds tissue adaptation capacity. The CELM integrates primary loading factors with protective and modifying factors, emphasizing the interaction between exposure, recovery, load distribution, and biological adaptation rather than a single causative mechanism. Direct evidence linking tennis ball characteristics to elbow injury remains limited, and the CELM should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating rather than predictive. This framework may provide a basis for clinical reasoning and future research examining the complex interaction among workload, biomechanics, fatigue, recovery, and tissue adaptation in tennis-related elbow disorders. # Level of Evidence 5.
journal: International journal of sports physical therapy

title: Neurocognitive Factors in ACL Injury: The Missing Piece in Rehabilitation and Prevention? A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Increasing evidence suggests that ACL injury should not be classified solely as a musculoskeletal condition, but rather as a neurophysiological injury. Several neurocognitive domains, including dual-task interference, visual attention, reaction time and cognitive fatigue, have been proposed as contributors to ACL injury. However, no studies have looked to explore subsections of these neurocognitive domains and their proposed mechanisms into prevention and injury risk. The purpose of this scoping review was to investigate the role of neurocognitive tasks in ACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review.
METHODS: The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR Checklist). Literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus and PEDro databases for studies published between 2006 and 2026. Search terms included combinations of "ACL", "dual-task", "neurocognitive", "reaction time", "visual attention", "decision making", "mental fatigue", "processing speed", and "cognitive interference". Screening was performed by a single reviewer, including publications at all levels of evidence, published in English or Italian.
RESULTS: Forty-two studies were included in the review. Dual-task interference and visual attention were the most investigated neurocognitive domains, with nine studies combining dual-task interference and visual attention and 10 studies combining dual-task interference, visual attention and reaction time. Six studies examined dual-task interference alone, five studies examined visual attention alone, and three studies examined reaction time alone. Cognitive fatigue was examined either alone or combined with other domains in seven studies. Neurocognitive training interventions demonstrated potential benefits in improving visuomotor efficiency, movement compliance and return to sport readiness after ACL rehabilitation. However, current evidence is predominantly derived from laboratory-based and exploratory studies with limited prospective and clinically translational data.
CONCLUSIONS: Neurocognitive factors appear to represent one of the major missing components in current ACL rehabilitation and prevention frameworks. Integrating neurocognitive challenges into rehabilitation and RTS testing may help clinicians better identify athletes at risk for secondary injury. Future research should prioritize prospective, clinically translational studies, as current evidence is predominantly exploratory and laboratory based.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 3.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Tendon Dry Needling for Recalcitrant Distal Biceps Tendinopathy: A Case Series.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Distal biceps brachii insertional tendinopathy occurs in approximately 2.6 per 100,000 individuals per year, more commonly affecting middle-aged males. Dry needling with percutaneous tendon fenestration is a common treatment for insertional tendinopathies. However, little evidence supports this treatment for the distal biceps tendon, likely secondary to difficult access without ultrasound guidance. This case series describes the treatment of two subjects with chronic distal biceps tendinopathy using ultrasound-guided percutaneous tendon dry needling with fenestration and a graded loading program in outpatient physical therapy.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series.
METHODS: Two recreationally active adults with chronic distal biceps tendon pathology underwent clinical and sonographic examination, with images reviewed by clinicians registered in musculoskeletal sonography (RMSK). Subject A (55 years of age) presented with a partial distal biceps tendon tear, and Subject B (46 years of age) presented with distal biceps tendinosis. Both had pain and exercise-related functional limitations, and each participated in a physical therapy plan of care consisting of one visit per week for five weeks, including ultrasound-guided tendon dry needling for the first three weeks and graded isotonic loading of the distal biceps tendon throughout. Each subject transitioned to a guided home exercise program and was reassessed 3 and 6 months from the evaluation date. Subject-reported outcome measures included the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), the Upper Extremity Functional Index (UEFI-20), and the Global Rating of Change (GROC) at baseline, 5 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months.
RESULTS: At five weeks, both subjects exceeded the minimal clinically important difference for each outcome measure. These results persisted at six months, with notable tendon healing characteristics visualized with diagnostic ultrasound.
CONCLUSIONS: Percutaneous ultrasound-guided tendon dry needling with fenestration as an adjunct to a graded tendon loading program may have contributed to reduced pain and disability among two individuals with distal biceps tendinopathy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.
journal: International journal of sports physical therapy

title: Minimally Invasive Zadek Osteotomy vs Open Achilles Debridement for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common cause of posterior heel pain in athletic populations and may require surgical intervention following failed conservative management. Minimally invasive Zadek osteotomy (MIS Zadek) has emerged as an alternative to traditional open Achilles tendon debridement with Haglund resection, with potential advantages in recovery and complication profile.
METHODS: A retrospective comparative cohort study was performed including 50 athletic patients with IAT (25 MIS Zadek, 25 open surgery) treated between 2022 and 2024 at a single high-volume centre. All patients participated in regular sports activity and failed at least 6 months of nonoperative treatment. The primary outcome was time to return to sport. Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport rate, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function (PF), PROMIS pain interference (PI), and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders.
RESULTS: Return to sport was achieved in 100% of MIS patients (25/25) and 92% of open patients (23/25; P = .49). Time to return to sport was shorter following MIS Zadek (4.3 ± 1.2 vs 6.1 ± 1.5 months; mean difference -1.8 months, 95% CI -2.6 to -1.0; P < .001). MIS remained independently associated with faster return to sport (adjusted β = -1.6 months, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.8; P < .001). Both groups showed substantial and clinically meaningful improvements in PROMIS outcomes. At 6 months, PROMIS PF was higher in the MIS group (56.5 ± 5.8 vs 52.3 ± 6.4; mean difference +4.2, 95% CI 0.6-7.8; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.69), with a similar pattern for PROMIS PI (47.2 ± 5.5 vs 51.1 ± 6.0; mean difference -3.9, 95% CI -7.1 to -0.7; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.67). By 18 months, PROMIS PF improved further in both groups with comparable outcomes (59.4 ± 4.9 vs 57.8 ± 5.2; mean difference +1.6, 95% CI -1.4 to 4.6; P = .29), and PROMIS PI similarly converged (44.8 ± 4.9 vs 46.3 ± 5.1; mean difference -1.5, 95% CI -4.4 to 1.4; P = .30). Complication rates were lower in the MIS group (2/25, 8%) compared with the open group (6/25, 24%; P = .25), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
CONCLUSION: MIS Zadek osteotomy was associated with faster return to sport and improved early recovery compared with open surgery; with the numbers available, no significant difference in long-term functional outcomes could be detected. Complications were numerically less frequent following MIS Zadek osteotomy, although this difference did not reach statistical significanceLevel of Evidence:Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: All-Inside Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Achilles Allograft and Suture Tape Augmentation.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction is challenged by graft elongation and delayed biological integration, often necessitating slow rehabilitation and carrying a risk of arthrofibrosis. This technical report describes an all-inside technique augmented with the modified internal bracing to address these limitations. The technique involves integrating a FiberTape within a quadrupled Achilles tendon allograft, creating a load-sharing composite. An all-inside, retrograde socket method was used for anatomic PCL reconstruction in the knee, with suspensory fixation on both femur and tibia. The graft-tape construct was simultaneously tensioned. The technique provides immediate biomechanical stability by mitigating graft micromotion, elongation, and tunnel abrasion. By closely replicating native PCL stiffness, this construct facilitates an accelerated, protective rehabilitation protocol focused on early motion and quadriceps activation, thereby aiming to reduce failure rates and postoperative stiffness. This method represents a synergistic evolution in PCL reconstruction, combining synthetic reinforcement with biological healing.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction and rehabilitation.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and oscillatory power.
RESULTS: Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy (d = 0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the prestimulus phase (d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials (d = 0.48), indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta (d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression (d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high uncertainty conditions.
CONCLUSION: Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into return-to-sport protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.

title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height.
METHODS: Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations.
RESULTS: Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006).
CONCLUSION: Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups.
METHODS: Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.
journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research

title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT.
CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks).

title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Athletes: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic Challenges, Management Strategies, and Return-to-Play Outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a compression disorder involving the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, or subclavian vein within the thoracic outlet. Athletes represent a distinct population in whom delayed diagnosis may result in career-threatening injuries.
OBJECTIVES: This review aimed to: (i) identify diagnostic pitfalls in athletes not captured by conventional provocative tests; (ii) evaluate conservative and operative management by TOS subtype; (iii) synthesize return-to-play (RTP) rates, timelines, and clearance criteria; and (iv) highlight methodological limitations and propose minimum reporting standards for future athlete-specific studies.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to July 2026 using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for TOS, its subtypes, Paget-Schroetter syndrome, and athletic populations. Reference lists were hand-searched. Studies addressing TOS diagnosis, classification, pathophysiology, management, or RTP in athletes were eligible regardless of design, reflecting limited randomized evidence. Journal legitimacy was screened using the Kscien's list.
RESULTS: nTOS is the predominant form in athletes and usually improves with 4-6 months of rehabilitation, whereas refractory cases may require surgery. vTOS/Paget-Schroetter syndrome requires urgent thrombolysis and early first-rib resection; aTOS is rare but limb-threatening and requires prompt surgery. Mixed presentations occur in up to 23% of surgical cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Outcomes are favorable with subtype-specific diagnosis and objective RTP criteria. However, evidence is limited by retrospective, single-center studies with pooled subtypes, inconsistent RTP definitions, and selective reporting. Prospective, sport-specific studies using standardized outcomes are needed.

title: When Athletes Ask About Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy.
abstract: Athletes exposed to repetitive head impacts (RHI) may seek clinical evaluation because of concerns about chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neuropathologically defined disease that cannot currently be diagnosed during life. As public awareness of CTE has expanded, clinicians face challenges communicating diagnostic uncertainty, interpreting non-specific symptoms, and addressing concerns about future neurological health. This Current Opinion examines the widening gap between public expectations and scientific capability and considers its implications for athlete-centered care. We discuss how clinicians can acknowledge uncertainty without dismissing patients' concerns, identify potentially treatable contributors to symptoms without prematurely attributing them to neurodegenerative disease, and use shared decision-making to guide individualized evaluation and management. We also consider how concerns about CTE may influence decisions about continued participation and return-to-sport among current athletes. Meeting these challenges requires coordinated interdisciplinary care, evidence-based communication, and clinical approaches that prioritize meaningful intervention even when diagnostic certainty remains unavailable.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.
