title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: Are both hemolysis and impaired myocyte integrity associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
abstract: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is a potent antioxidant enzyme. G6PD deficiency, predominant among males, is a neonatal "neurotoxic" risk, characterized by episodic hemolysis that is sometimes infection triggered. Clinical risk among heterozygous G6PD-deficient females is often under-recognized. Recent reports of rhabdomyolysis among G6PD-deficient individuals are reviewed here. In one case, a male athlete with G6PD deficiency (<10% activity) experienced multiple, acute episodes of rhabdomyolysis, painful muscle symptomatology, injury and hemolysis after strenuous exertion. Both his mother with G6PD-deficiency (<45% activity) and maternal grandmother have chronic histories of episodic or triggered fatigue-related disruptive symptoms. Other case reports of G6PD-deficient individuals with muscle injury and exertional symptoms (with or without hemolysis) showed unique laboratory findings of elevated creatine kinase, myoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, and aminotransferases levels and myoglobinuria. Disrupted myocyte energetics and loss of cellular integrity can be attributed to impaired downstream pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)-related oxidant stress protection, which is a key enzymatic consequence of G6PD-deficiency. These triggered stresses may explain the muscle fatigue and propensity to exertional injury. Correlation between stress-sensitive-impaired muscle injury among all G6PD-deficient individuals, including neonates, requires further clinical validation to ascertain oxidant-stress impact of impaired PPP-dependent cellular energetics of red blood, white blood, neural, and muscle cells.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Beware the Muscle: Silent Exercise-Induced Aminotransferase Elevation as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Hepatology and Pretreatment Screening-A Report of Two Cases.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In clinical hepatology practice, pretreatment liver enzyme screening plays a key role in making management decisions, such as initiation of antituberculosis therapy or surveillance of chronic hepatitis B. Unrecognized extrahepatic sources of aminotransferase elevations can lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate treatment alteration, and unnecessary invasive or costly investigations.
CASE PRESENTATION: We present two cases of active young males who were undergoing liver biochemical testing for therapeutic decision-making for other underlying illnesses. Patient one was undergoing baseline liver enzyme testing prior to first-line antituberculosis treatment initiation while patient two was undergoing surveillance for e-antigen-negative hepatitis B infection. Both patients had asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations mimicking acute hepatocellular injury. There was a marked and disproportionate elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) relative to alanine aminotransferase (ALT), in the setting of otherwise normal cholestatic and synthetic parameters. Targeted history revealed heavy resistance weight training prior to testing. Measurement of serum creatine kinase (CK) confirmed exercise-induced muscle injury, demonstrating elevated CK concentrations that paralleled the AST trajectory. Cessation of strenuous training led to rapid normalization of aminotransferases and a decline in CK levels, without interruption of tuberculosis management or unwarranted antiviral initiation.
CONCLUSION: Clinically silent exertional muscle injury is an underappreciated mimicker of acute liver injury. In patients presenting with isolated or disproportionate AST elevation, confirming a myogenic enzyme source via CK quantification can prevent misdiagnosis, eliminate unnecessary liver-directed workup, and avoid inappropriate modification or initiation of essential pharmacotherapy.

title: Role of integrin αvβ5 receptor and microglia in delayed-onset muscle soreness in mice.
abstract: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is characterized by muscle pain, stiffness, and tenderness following intense or unaccustomed exercise. In humans, symptoms typically arise 6-72 h post-exercise. This study investigated a novel mechanism underlying DOMS, focusing on the involvement of the irisin receptor integrin αvβ5 and spinal microglia in its development. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to a DOMS model induced by an acute aerobic exercise protocol, and nociceptive thresholds were assessed using the von Frey filament test. The role of spinal integrin αvβ5 was evaluated via intrathecal administration of the antagonist cilengitide, given both prior to exercise and 24 h post-exercise. To assess irisin's nociceptive effects, it was also administered intrathecally. Additionally, minocycline, a microglial inhibitor, was administered before irisin to determine microglial involvement. An in vitro assay evaluated microglial activation by irisin via flow cytometry. Pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines were quantified by ELISA. Cilengitide reversed exercise-induced DOMS and reduced spinal pro-inflammatory cytokines. Irisin induced nociception, which was attenuated by minocycline. Irisin also activated microglia in vitro, increasing pro-inflammatory cytokine production. These findings suggest integrin αvβ5 and spinal microglia play critical roles in DOMS pathogenesis, with irisin and pro-inflammatory cytokines as key mediators.
journal: Journal of muscle research and cell motility

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery: Are Marathon and Trail Running Different?
abstract: Although trail and road are two running disciplines, they have distinct characteristics potentially leading to different physiological impacts that have never been examined. The aim of the present study was to compare neuromuscular fatigue and recovery between a marathon and two trail runs of equivalent effort (29 km; ± 1,400 m). Forty-one trained runners, specialized in either road or trail running, performed a simulated treadmill marathon (MARASIM), a simulated treadmill trail run (TRAILSIM), or a trail run in natural conditions (TRAILNAT), depending on their speciality. Neuromuscular fatigue, i.e. changes in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), voluntary activation (VA) and peak twitch (Tw) of the knee extensors (KE) and plantar flexors (PF), blood markers of muscle damage, jump performance, and force-velocity profile (FVP) were assessed before (PRE), immediately after (POST), one (+1 day), two (+2 days), and seven days (+7 days) following the runs. Muscle pain questionnaires were administered at PRE and during the month following the run. MARASIM showed significantly greater decreases in KE VA (-23.5% vs. -9.2% vs. -13.0%) and jump height (-11.7%; +11.4%; +5.9%, for squat jump), and significantly higher increases in blood markers of muscle damage (+1,726 UI.L -1; +641 UI.L -1; +363 UI.L -1; at +1 day) compared to TRAILSIM and TRAILNAT, respectively. The return to baseline occurred later in MARASIM for KE VA and jump height. Muscle soreness values also returned to baseline earlier in TRAILNAT and TRAILSIM compared to MARASIM. No differences between groups existed in KE Pt and MVC, in any PF neuromuscular fatigue variables, and FVP. Overall, marathon running appears to induce greater acute neuromuscular alterations than trail running, mostly on KE, with a slower return to baseline values.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Evaluation of a four-herb Chinese medicine formula at different concentrations on muscle damage and inflammation in a rat model of DOMS.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) impairs exercise recovery, while current treatments remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) formulas may provide safe, multi-target interventions.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the dose-dependent protective effects of a four-herb Chinese medicine formulation (safflower, Chinese Angelica, peach kernel and myrrh) against DOMS in a rat model.
METHODS: Thirty-two male SPF SD rats were randomly allocated to control or low- (1696 mg/kg), medium- (3392 mg/kg), or high-dose (6784 mg/kg) groups. The formulation was administered orally for 11 days, with DOMS induced by exhaustive swimming on day 8. Serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-exercise.
RESULTS: The medium- and high-dose groups exhibited significantly lower serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 levels than controls, with the high-dose group showing the largest reductions. The low-dose group showed limited or no significant reductions in most markers, demonstrating a clear dose-dependent protective effect.
CONCLUSIONS: The formulation dose-dependently attenuates muscle damage and inflammation in a rat DOMS model, with high-dose treatment achieving the fastest recovery. Clinical trials are warranted to confirm the efficacy and safety in humans.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels.
METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group.
RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels.
CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

title: Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury initiates biological processes linked to joint tissue degeneration. The longitudinal time course of serum biomarkers reflecting inflammation and cartilage metabolism after ACL reconstruction (ACLR), particularly in comparison with uninjured controls, has not been characterized across the first postoperative year.
HYPOTHESIS: Inflammatory (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 [MCP-1]) and degradative (matrix metalloproteinase-3 [MMP-3]) biomarker concentrations would be elevated pre-ACLR and decrease over time, whereas cartilage turnover biomarker concentrations (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein [COMP] and type II collagen degradation-to-synthesis ratio [C2C:CPII]) would increase postoperatively. Also, pre-ACLR biomarker concentrations would be associated with concentrations at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: A total of 33 individuals with ACL injuries (52% female; mean age, 20.8 ± 2.4 years) were evaluated pre-ACLR and at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. A total of 33 matched uninjured controls were included. Serum concentrations of MCP-1, MMP-3, COMP, and C2C:CPII were assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Linear mixed-effects models with model-based contrasts were used to evaluate differences across groups and time points. ACLR-only linear mixed-effects regression models were used to assess associations between pre-ACLR and follow-up biomarker concentrations. Exploratory post hoc models evaluated differences by concomitant injury status.
RESULTS: MCP-1 was elevated in individuals with ACL injuries compared with controls at all ACLR time points (all Padj < .001), with no change across ACLR time points. MMP-3 increased from pre-ACLR to 6 months post-ACLR (Padj < .001) but did not differ from controls at any time point. COMP was consistently greater in individuals with ACL injuries than in controls at all time points (all Padj≤ .021), with no changes across ACLR time points. C2C:CPII was greater at 12 months post-ACLR than at pre-ACLR and 6 months post-ACLR (both Padj < .001) and than in uninjured controls (Padj = .001). Pre-ACLR MCP-1, MMP-3, and COMP concentrations were associated with concentrations at both 6 and 12 months post-ACLR (all P≤ .006), whereas C2C:CPII was associated only with 12-month concentrations (P = .018).
CONCLUSION: Inflammatory and cartilage-related biomarkers remain altered throughout the first year after ACLR, suggesting that the biological response is not fully resolved by reconstruction and standard rehabilitation but extends beyond the early postoperative period.
journal: The American journal of sports medicine

title: Balneotherapy in knee osteoarthritis: a review of therapeutic efficacy and inflammatory cytokine regulation.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a common degenerative joint disease with an inflammatory component. Balneotherapy has been used for KOA, but its clinical efficacy and mechanisms remain uncertain. This narrative review summarizes clinical evidence and proposes a hypothesis-generating mechanistic framework. PubMed and CNKI were searched up to June 2026. Interventions were categorized as mineral-water bathing, aquatic exercise/hydrotherapy, mud therapy/pelotherapy, or multimodal spa programmes, and clinical studies were assessed for risk of bias. Randomized trials and meta-analyses suggest that balneotherapy may improve short-term pain and function, with benefits reportedly persisting for 3-9 months in some studies; however, most trials had high risk of bias, heterogeneous protocols, small samples, and short follow-up. Mechanistic evidence is largely preclinical or indirect. H₂S has the most consistent anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic rationale, acting via NF-κB and MMP-13 inhibition. Calcium and magnesium may modulate TRPV4/NLRP3 and NF-κB signaling, but human balneotherapy evidence is lacking, and mineral synergy remains unverified. A three-tier "heat-mineral-signal" framework is proposed, but target engagement after bathing and causality between biomarker changes and clinical improvement have not been established. Overall, balneotherapy may offer symptomatic benefits in KOA, but current evidence is limited and heterogeneous. The proposed mechanistic model is hypothesis-generating; higher-quality trials with standardized protocols, long-term follow-up, and integrated clinical and mechanistic outcomes are needed.

title: Acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery after total knee arthroplasty in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery in older adults following total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating acupuncture or electroacupuncture for postoperative outcomes in adults undergoing TKA. Primary outcomes included pain intensity (Visual Analogue Scale [VAS]) and functional outcomes (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index [WOMAC], Hospital for Special Surgery [HSS] score, and range of motion). Secondary outcomes included analgesic consumption and adverse events.
RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs involving 1037 participants were included. Acupuncture and electroacupuncture were associated with reduced postoperative pain (VAS: SMD = -1.08, 95% CI, -1.27 to -0.89; Z = 11.09; p < 0.00001) and improved functional outcomes (HSS: SMD = 1.39, 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.75; Z = 7.48; p < 0.00001). No serious adverse events were reported in the included studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Acupuncture may provide beneficial effects on postoperative pain and selected functional outcomes after TKA in older adults. Given the multidisciplinary nature of postoperative recovery, these findings may be relevant to geriatric nursing care, particularly in pain assessment, rehabilitation coordination, and monitoring of recovery. However, the available evidence does not establish acupuncture as a nurse-led intervention.

title: The gut-muscle-joint axis in osteoarthritis: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Emerging evidence highlights a complex crosstalk between the gut microbiota, musculoskeletal tissues, and the joint microenvironment, revealing osteoarthritis (OA) as a systemic disorder rather than a localized cartilage disease. The gut-muscle-joint interaction integrates microbial dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation to influence cartilage homeostasis, muscle strength, and neuromuscular stability. Building upon previously described gut-osteoarthritis and gut-muscle interactions, the Gut-Muscle-Joint (GMJ) axis is presented as an integrative framework linking intestinal permeability, microbial metabolites, systemic inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular health, skeletal muscle function, and joint integrity. Perturbations in this axis amplify oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix degradation across musculoskeletal tissues. Understanding GMJ axis-driven mechanisms offers novel preventive and therapeutic strategies that target microbiome restoration, metabolic reprogramming, and neuromuscular health through probiotics, postbiotics, AMPK-SIRT1 activators, and structured exercise. This integrative perspective positions the GMJ axis as a unifying framework for intervention, enabling precision approaches to preserve joint function, reduce sarcopenia, and attenuate OA progression.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

title: Multimodal rehabilitation interventions reduce pain in dogs with osteoarthritis, regardless of enrollment in formal in-clinic or outpatient rehabilitation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The objective was to determine the effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on Canine Brief Pain Inventory (CBPI) pain scores in dogs diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA), and to determine whether effects differed between formal in-clinic versus outpatient rehabilitation.
ANIMALS AND PROCEDURE: Medical records from between 2022 and 2024 were reviewed for dogs with OA that were presented to a rehabilitation specialist. Each dog's caregiver completed a CBPI at both the initial evaluation and 1st follow-up visit. Dogs were allocated into 2 groups: those that received in-clinic rehabilitation and those that received outpatient interventions. Both groups received customized, multimodal plans to address their OA signs. Pain severity scores (PSS), pain interference scores (PIS), and overall interference scores were compared between groups. A 2-sample Student's t-test or a Fisher's exact test was used to compare groups, with a statistical significance level of 0.05.
RESULTS: A total of 79 dogs were included in the study. There were no differences between dogs enrolled in in-clinic rehabilitation versus outpatient rehabilitation for sex, age, weight, or body condition score (P = 0.541, P = 0.26, P = 0.58, P = 0.33, respectively). The PSS and PIS had improved at the 1st recheck in both groups (in-clinic: P = 0.01 and P = 0.03; outpatient: P = 0.03 and P = 0.03, respectively).
CONCLUSION AND CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Owner-perceived pain decreased in all dogs, whether they were enrolled in formal in-clinic rehabilitation or not. This was attributed to customized interventions, including rehabilitation, pain management, and weight management. Our results corroborated reports that multimodal OA management plans, including rehabilitation interventions, ameliorate symptoms of OA in humans. Given the high prevalence of canine OA, this study supported the beneficial effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on the well-being of osteoarthritic dogs.
journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Return to Sport After Foot and Ankle Surgery Is Inconsistently Defined and Assessed: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To conduct a systematic review of return-to-sport (RTS) definitions in the orthopaedic literature, addressing common operative athletic foot and ankle pathologies including ankle instability, Achilles tendon ruptures or tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fractures.
METHODS: A systematic review was performed in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Cochrane, Embase, Medline, and CINAHL databases were searched for studies published through March 2024. Inclusion criteria were studies in which subjects were involved in some level of sports and received surgery for 1 of 3 common sports-related injuries: ankle instability, Achilles tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fracture. The primary outcome was each study's definition of RTS.
RESULTS: There were 145 articles that met all inclusion criteria. Of these, 73 articles investigated ankle instability, 56 investigated Achilles tendinopathy, and 16 investigated fifth metatarsal fracture. Seventy-nine articles (54.5%) had an unclear definition of RTS with 66 articles (45.5%) reporting a precise definition. Sixty-four articles (44.1%) provided an isolated binary metric reporting whether a patient returned to sport or failed to provide a method for determining the timepoint for RTS. Thirty-eight (26.2%) of the articles used an objective start criterion (e.g., resumption of competition), followed by custom (n = 27, 18.6%) and standardized patient-reported questionnaire use (n = 21, 14.5%).
CONCLUSIONS: Most articles included in this systematic review did not provide an explicit definition of RTS or a clearly defined assessment methodology. When specified, RTS was assessed using objective events, custom questionnaires, or standardized patient-reported outcome measures, highlighting substantial heterogeneity in both RTS definitions and assessment approaches across foot and ankle literature.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level I to IV studies.

title: Quadriceps Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Mechanisms of Weakness and Evidence-Based Rehabilitation Strategies.
abstract: Impairment of quadriceps strength is a frequent and clinically important problem after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and reconstruction. This dysfunction reflects muscular, neural, surgical, and rehabilitation-related mechanisms and is not solely attributable to muscle atrophy. Despite restoration of joint stability, quadriceps weakness can persist and contribute to delayed functional recovery and reduced readiness to return to sport. A comprehensive assessment should integrate clinical examination, objective isometric or isokinetic strength testing, rate of force development, functional performance, quality of movement, imaging investigations, and patient-reported and psychological measures. Rehabilitation should be initiated preoperatively and continue postoperatively with a focus on control of effusion and restoration of extension, early quadriceps activation, progressive resistance exercise, appropriate open-chain loading followed by eccentric, plyometric, and sport-specific training. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation has supportive evidence as an adjunct, and blood-flow restriction training may be useful when higher loads may not yet be tolerated. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the mechanisms and rehabilitation of quadriceps weakness after ACL injury and ACL reconstruction, highlighting clinically relevant strategies for restoring strength and neuromuscular function.

title: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: We read with interest the recent article by Barrera Uso et al. on early arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The study provides clinically relevant evidence that AMI at 30 days strongly predicts persistence at 60 days. We suggest, however, that this finding should be interpreted as a prognostic association rather than evidence that 30-day AMI is the dominant biological determinant of subsequent inhibition. We also discuss the timing of postoperative assessment, noting that evaluation at 30 days is appropriate for studying persistence but less informative regarding the initial pathophysiological development of AMI. The Scientific Anterior Cruciate Ligament Network International (SANTI) classification has demonstrated excellent reliability in anterior cruciate ligament populations, although its generalizability to TKA remains to be specifically established. Finally, the absence of objective functional and patient-reported outcomes limits interpretation of the clinical significance of persistent AMI. Overall, the study identifies an important clinical phenotype and useful prognostic markers while leaving the underlying mechanisms of persistence to be further clarified.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. This article presents a case of recurrent flexor tendon failure in a young manual laborer, detailing initial repair, rupture, and secondary reconstruction. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.
journal: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America

title: Exostosis of the sustentaculum tali causing tibiotarsal joint pathology in a Standardbred racehorse trotter.
abstract: This report describes a novel case of exostosis on the medial aspect of the sustentaculum tali, (ST) associated with tibiotarsal joint (TTJ) pathology, without involvement of the tarsal sheath or lateral digital flexor tendon. A 5-year-old Standardbred gelding was presented with right TTJ effusion and exercise-induced hind-limb lameness. Diagnostic imaging identified a columnar periosteal proliferation on the medial ST, accompanied by synovial effusion and joint capsule thickening; however, the tarsal sheath and lateral digital flexor tendon remained unremarkable. Although TTJ arthroscopy confirmed synovitis, it did not allow visualization of the exostosis. The lesion was successfully excised via an ultrasound-guided extra-articular surgical approach. Postoperative management included a structured rehabilitation program, resulting in a return to full-speed training by Day 76 with no recurrence of lameness. Follow-up evaluations demonstrated improved performance and complete resolution of TTJ effusion and associated swelling. This case highlighted the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying extra-synovial lesions of the ST and supported ultrasound-guided extra-articular removal as an effective surgical option for ST exostosis. Although the underlying cause of the lesion was uncertain, subclinical trauma was considered a likely contributing factor. Key clinical message: The ST is a horizontal bony projection on the plantaromedial aspect of the calcaneus. Due to its minimal soft-tissue coverage, it is particularly vulnerable to external trauma and subsequent osseous proliferation. Exostosis of the ST may result in impingement of the plantaromedial pouch of the tarsocrural (tibiotarsal) joint, contributing to joint irritation and secondary pathology. Accurate diagnosis and effective case management rely on the combined use of radiography and ultrasonography, which together enable detailed assessment of both osseous changes and associated soft-tissue structures.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.
journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.
journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
abstract: Rebelo, A, Ripley, N, Weakley, J, and Comfort, P. Relationships between isometric belt squat force and vertical jump performance across knee joint angles. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the relationships between vertical jump performance and isometric belt squat force assessed at 2 knee joint angles (120° and 90°) and to compare outcomes across age groups in male and female athletes. One hundred and twenty subjects (20.3 ± 6.5 years, 1.77 ± 0.12 m, 71.0 ± 13.3 kg) performed countermovement jumps, squat jumps, and isometric belt squat tests at 120° and 90° on dual force platforms. Between-group differences were analyzed using 1-way or Welch's analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses. Associations were examined using Pearson's correlations with Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds (p < 0.002), while omnibus tests used corrected alpha levels where applicable. Isometric belt squat net peak force demonstrated weak-to-moderate associations with jump height across tasks (r = 0.36-0.55). Associations between net force at 200 milliseconds and jump height were moderate at 90° (r = 0.45-0.52), whereas net force at 100 milliseconds showed negligible associations to jump height. Older athletes produced significantly higher absolute isometric net peak force than younger groups only at 90° knee flexion (up to ∼860 N difference), with moderate-to-large effects (g = 0.67-0.80), whereas relative net peak force did not differ between age categories. These findings indicate that the isometric belt squat can be confidently used to monitor maximal lower-limb force capacity across knee angles, with the 90° position offering greater sensitivity for distinguishing strength levels between age groups.
journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research

title: Shallow under load? Prevalence of acetabular morphologies and their association with sport exposure during skeletal maturation in professional female football players: a retrospective study using data from the PROFE cohort.
abstract: We aimed to report the prevalence of acetabular morphologies in professional female footballers and explore the association between these morphologies and sport exposure during the period of skeletal maturation. 100 professional female footballers (200 hips) were included. Athletes with a history of systemic disease were excluded. Questionnaires obtained information on previous sport frequencies and age of menarche. Participants reported the minimum hours of sport played weekly during three age categories/stages of growth: cartilaginous hypertrophy (8-10 years), skeletal growth (11-12 years), and closure of growth plates (13-16 years). Participants underwent a pelvic radiograph. The Wiberg-center edge angle classified hips with normal coverage, borderline dysplasia, dysplasia or pincer morphology. Logistic regression models explored the association between prevalence of acetabular morphologies and minimum of sport hours played weekly in different age groups. Interactions with age of menarche were explored. From 200 hips, 32% were classified as having borderline dysplasia, 9% had dysplasia, 1% had pincer morphology, and 58% had normal coverage. Athletes with a later age of menarche had higher odds of dysplasia with increasing sport exposure between 8-10 (OR [95%CI] = 1.23 [1.05-1.44]). p = 0.011) and 11-12 years (OR [95%CI] = 1.21 [1.06-1.38], p = 0.006) compared to those with an earlier age of menarche. Skeletal maturation might be an important period for the development of acetabular morphology in female footballers. Exposure to high‑load sport activity during skeletal maturation and age of menarche may contribute to the development of hip dysplasia in these athletes.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Gender Differences in Sports Injuries of the Foot and Ankle.
abstract: This article examines sex-based differences in foot and ankle injuries among female athletes, emphasizing the role of anatomic, hormonal, biomechanical, and sociocultural factors. Female athletes are disproportionately affected by ankle sprains, chronic instability, and bone stress injuries. Conditions such as relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad contribute to injury risk and long-term health consequences but remain under-recognized. This article highlights disparities in research, treatment, and outcomes, calling for improved screening, sex-specific prevention strategies, and greater inclusion of female subjects in sports medicine research to inform evidence-based care and optimize outcomes for female athletes.

title: Metabolic Bone Health in Female Patients: Focus on Foot and Ankle.
abstract: Metabolic bone health is crucial for the overall well-being of female patients. Female athletes and young females are of particular interest, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are sensitive to the hormonal and physical stress of training and diet. Stress fractures occur with higher frequency in females with risk factors such as low bone mineral density (BMD). When low bone mineral density occurs along with menstrual irregularities and relative energy deficiency, it completes the female triad (23, 27, and 28). Any discussion of female BMD and metabolic bone health must include the female triad.
